full_judgment:
2. The opposite party No.1, while alive, and his wife, the opposite party No. 2, instituted the aforesaid suit as plaintiffs on the averments, inter alia, that a piece and parcel of land measuring 6.76 acres of C.S. Plot Nos.1145, 1170, 1171, 1350, 1351, 1352 and 1416 of mouza Khilgaon, formerly P.S. Tejgaon, now Motijhcel, Dhaka was and is owned by them which was requisitioned in L.A Case No. 63/59-60 by a notice dated 21.6.60 under section 3 of the Emergency Requisition of Property Act, 1948 for the defendant-opposite party No. 3, the Railway Board. The requisitioning authority tool over possession of the suit land from the opposing parties on 21.6.60. The suit land was requisitioned with the object of permanent acquisition, but no notice under section 5(1a) and (3) was served "either in the locality or on the plaintiffs as required by law for acquisition". An Additional Deputy Commissioner (Development) passed an order to serve fresh notices on the opposite parties under the said sections, being satisfied that no such notices were served before, but the file mysteriously disappeared. On 13.9.67 the successor Additional Deputy Commissioner noting that an injustice will be committed by depriving the opposite parties of due compensation, passed an order to serve fresh notices on the plaintiff opposite parties. But the officers concerned having dragged their feet in the matter of serving fresh notices the plaintiff opposite parties were constrained to file a' suit being Title Suit No. 36 of 1968 in the 1st Court of Munsif, Dhaka against the defendant-petitioners and the opposite party No. 3 challenging their claim of acquisition of the suit land without service of legal notices under section 5(1a) and 5(3) of Act-XIII of 1948. The present defendant-petitioners contested the suit by filing a written statement and by asserting that the said notices have been duly served upon the plaintiff-opposite parties. By his judgment and decree dated 8.7.69 the learned Munsif decreed the suit in favour of the plaintiff-opposite parties. The learned Munsif came to the conclusion that notices under section 5(1a) and 5(3) of the said Act were not served on the plaintiffs and as such there was no valid acquisition of the disputed property. 

 3. Against the said judgment and decree the defendant-petitioners preferred Title Appeal No.28 of 1970 in the Court of District Judge, Dhaka who by his judgment and decree dated 24.5.71 dismissed the appeal and affirmed the judgment and decree of the learned Munsif. The plaintiff-opposite parties thus became entitled to fresh notices for valid and legal acquisition of the suit land. 

 4. Instead of issuing fresh notices the defendant- petitioners formulated a fraudulent device to serve a copy of the alleged original notice under section 5(1) dated 21.6.60 putting a fresh date of issue in the notice under section 5(1a). This alleged copy of the old original notice under section 5(1) of the said Act was served on 23.4.73 directing the plaintiff-opposite parties to appear before the concerned authority on 30.12.60 to object to the acquisition proceedings, if any. This action was fraudulent and absurd on the face of it. The defendant-petitioners also served a fresh notice under section 5(3) of the said Act on the same day, i.e. 23.4.73 upon the plaintiff-opposite parties giving 7 days' notice to object to the acquisition of the suit land. The statute requires the concerned authority to give notice of 15 days to state the owners' objection. But in the notice served on 23.4.73 the plaintiff-opposite parties were asked to file their objections on 30.4.73; i.e. within 7 days. This notice was also an illegal, invalid and void notice. 

 5. The plaintiff-opposite parties made representations against such wrong actions before various authorities including Mr. Mirza Golam Hafez who was the Minister-in-Charge of the Ministry of Land Administration & Land Reforms. After a detailed discussion of facts and law involved in the matter, he came to the view that there had been no legal or valid acquisition of the suit property as no notices under section 5(1a) and 5(3) were served. Upon the Minister's order an opinion was obtained from the Ministry of Law which also opined that fresh notices under section 5(la) and 5(3) were required to be served for valid acquisition of the suit property. Thereafter, Mr. Abdul Haque took over charge as Minister of Land Administration and Land Reforms, but before passing any written order in the matter he went out of office. His successor Mr. Md. Ismail passed an order simply rejecting the plaintiff-opposite parties representation. The plaintiff-opposite parties then submitted a representation on 12.3.82 to the then President of Bangladesh. Subsequently they made a representation on 4.6.82 to the Chief Martial Law Administrator and submitted all relevant papers. They received a communication in January, 1983 from the Secretariat of the Chief Martial Law Administrator advising them to seek relief in a civil Court. 

 (d) for an order of mandatory injunction directing the defendants to perform their statutory duties by making proper and lawful assessment for the period of requisition through requisition order dated 21.6.60 till the filing of the suit for use and occupation of the suit land as well as start valid acquisition proceeding afresh under Part-II, section 3 of the Acquisition & Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982 and other provisions of law in force for ex- pressed intent of acquisition within 3 months failing which the possession of the suit land be restored to the plaintiffs. 

 7. The defendant-petitioners filed a written statement and contested the suit. It was stated that there was no cause of action for the suit; that the suit was not maintainable in its present form and manner; that the suit was barred under sections 42 and 55 of the Specific Relief Act; that it was barred by the law of limitation; that it was barred by res judicata and also barred under the provisions of Act- XIII of 1948. It was stated that the plaintiffs' land measuring an area of 6.4650 acres along with other lands was requisitioned on 21.6.60 with a view to permanent acquisition for Railway Staff Quarter under L.A. Case No.63 of 1959-60. Vacant possession of the land in question was handed over to the requiring body on 2.7.60 and since then the Railway Board is possessing the suit land after constructing their buildings except approximately an area of 0.16 acre of land which is still under the occupation of the plaintiffs. The land in question has already been acquired and vested in the Government vide Gazette Notification No.DA-72/71/355 dated 25.6.73. From the office record of the office of Additional Deputy Commissioner (Land Acquisition) it appears vide order sheet at page 20 dated 30.12.60 that the notice under section 5(la) and 5(3) was issued to the plaintiffs in the year 1960. It was further stated that as per order of the then Additional Deputy Commissioner (Development) on the body of the report of the then Kanungo, the Ministry of Land Administration & Land Reforms was informed Vide T.O. No. 2095- L.A. dated 14.6.72 for a fresh requisition and acquisition of the land in question of the plaintiffs. The Ministry thereupon issued instructions along with the Attorney-General's minutes dated 15.3.73 where- upon the office of the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Land Acquisition) served upon the plaintiffs a fresh notice under section 5(3) fixing 30.4.73 for filing objection, if any, against acquisition along with the true copy of the notice under section 5(1a) as already served in the locality in the year 1960. It is claimed that the said Gazette Notification is quite legal, valid and binding upon the plaintiffs and the suit land vested in the defendants absolutely and free from any encumbrances with the publication of the aforesaid Notification. Fresh notice or fresh acquisition proceedings under the Acquisition & Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982 is neither necessary, nor can be conceived of in respect of the suit land which has already vested in the defendants. The object of filing of the suit is to get a fresh notice for fresh assessment of compensation causing loss and injury to the defendants. 

 9. The trial Court was of the view that if the disputed acquisition was invalid and ineffective in the eye of law, then the plaintiff-opposite parties were entitled to recovery of possession of the suit land at the time of institution of Title Suit No. 36 of 1968. But since they omitted that claim in the said suit, they have subjected themselves to the mischief of Order 2, Rule 2(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure. They have also invited the hurdle of limitation provided in Article 142 of the Limitation Act. 

 10. The trial Court, however, was clearly of the view that the subsequent fresh service of old notice cannot have any effect of legalizing an illegal acquisition. The disputed acquisition continued to be an invalid acquisition in spite of a ridiculous attempt on the part of the Government to validate it by a fresh service of an old notice. The Gazelle Notification dated 25.6.73 is devoid of any legal effect and, as such it had no effect of vesting the suit land with the Government under section 5(7) of Act-XIII of 1948, but the decree will be of no use to the plaintiffs in the absence of consequential relief in the form of recovery of possession etc. The plaintiffs have not sought any consequential relief. So the suit was barred under the proviso to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. The prayer No. (c) is practically covered by prayer No. (b). Hence, the prayer (c) also cannot be given. The prayer No. (d) is vague, indefinite and cumbrous. When there is no valid acquisition of the suit land, there cannot be any question of assessment of compensation. The plaintiff-opposite parties could seek recovery of possession of the suit land with mesne profits. 

 13. The appellate Court below concurrently held with the trial Court that the service of an alleged copy of the old original notice under section 5 (1) dated 21.6.60 after 13 years on 23.4.73 fixing 30.12.60 as the date of hearing under section 5(5) is completely unreasonable, impracticable and impossible. The intention of service of notice is not fulfilled thereby. Hence, it is invalid and illegal in the eye of law. Without serving a notice under section 5(1a) there cannot be any assessment of compensation for acquisition of land. The appellate Court below concurrently held with the trial Court that giving 7 days notice instead of 15 days in the notice under section 5 (3) is defective and illegal. The subsequent Gazette Notification issued in pursuance of an illegal and invalid course of action is also illegal and invalid. The appellate Court below then noticed some decisions and held that the entire acquisition proceeding was illegal, without jurisdiction and invalid. As such, the suit was decreed in so far as plaintiff-opposite parties prayer Nos. (b), (c) and (d) in the plaint were concerned. 

 17. The learned Deputy Attorney-General next submits, that the Court of appeal below has failed to evaluate the true meaning and import of the judgment and decree in Title Suit No. 36 of 1968. It is stated in the judgment, "it is the definite case of the plaintiffs that no notices under section 5(1 a) and 5(3) of the East Bengal (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948 were served on the plaintiffs before the alleged acquisition". It is also the finding that notices under section 5(la) and 5(3) "were not served on the plaintiffs" and as such there was no valid acquestion of the disputed property. Mr. Salehuzzamaa submits that this declaration conferred no real benefit to the plaintiffs and as such the copy of the original notice dated 21.6.60 was rightly served on them on 23.4.73. 

 5.(1a) The Deputy Commissioner shall, if he considers that the acquisition of any requisitioned property is expedient for a public purpose or in public interest, cause a public notice to be given at convenient places on or near the requisitioned property stating that the property is proposed to be acquired." 

 20. Mr. Salehuzzaman submits that in Title Suit No. 36. of 1968, all that the plaintiff-opposite parties obtained by way of a finding and by way of a decree is that notices under section 5(1a) and 5(3) "were not served on the plaintiffs". The Government took the view that the aforesaid declaration of the Court did not confer on the plaintiff-opposite parties any real benefit Had there been a declaration that no notice was issued under section 5(1a) or that such notice was illegal or invalid, the subsequent acquisition proceeding would have been materially affected, because the date of notice under section 5(1a) is relevant for determination of the market value of the acquired property for compensation. The Government took the view that notice under section 5(1a) is a general notice, so it is definitely not required to be served on the owner but the notice under section 5(3) is a personal notice and is required to be served on the owner. Therefore, the declaration in Title Suit No. 36 of 1968, in so far as it relates to notice under section 5(1a) being not served on the plaintiffs, seemed to be of no real effect and of no real value to the plaintiffs. This declaration in any view of the matter did not in terms invalidate or have the effect of invalidating the notice already issued under section 5(1a) in the connected land acquisition case. However, in view of the declaration made by the Court, a copy of the old original notice under section 5(1) dated 21.6.60 was served upon the plaintiff-opposite parties along with a fresh notice under section 5(3). Mr. Salehuzzaman submits that this was done in strict compliance with the meaning and purport of the declaratory decree obtained by the plaintiff- opposite parties in Title Suit No. 36 of 1968. It is true, he submits, that the notice under section 5(3) falls short of 8 days in giving the plaintiff-opposite parties an opportunity to file objections against the acquisition, if any, but the notice was issued by a competent authority with jurisdiction and whatever defect was there was a mere irregularity and did not strike at the very jurisdiction to issue the notice. The plaintiff-opposite parties could have represented to the authority complaining of shortage of time and the defect could have been remedied but they preferred not to file any objection and, therefore, the appellate Court below ought to have considered that both the old notice under section 5(1) and the new notice under section 5(3) were served in full compliance with the decree obtained by the plaintiff-opposite parties in Title Suit No. 36 of 1968. He further submits that the plaintiff-opposite parties have not challenged the competence or jurisdiction of the authorities to issue the notices under sections 5(1a) and 5 (3) and to issue the Gazette Notification dated 25.6.73. They have also not challenged the validity of public purpose for acquisition of the suit land. As such, he submits, the suit itself is barred under section 14A of Act No. XIII of 1948. 

 21. Mr. Gholam Rabbani, learned Advocate for the plaintiff-opposite parties, has read out to us paragraph 7 of the plaint in Title Suit No. 36 of 1968 in which the plaintiff-opposite parties clearly stated that there has been no due service of notice in the matter either in the locality or on the plaintiffs. He has also read out prayer No. (a) of the aforesaid plaint seeking a declaration that there has been no valid service of notice for acquisition under section 5(la) and 5(3) of Act No. XIII of 1948 with regard to the suit land in the connected land acquisition case. Therefore, the plaintiff-opposite parties themselves did not make out any case in the aforesaid Title Suit No.36 of 1968 that notice under section 5(1) or 5(1a) are required to be served personally on them and that they did not receive any personal notices under those sections. They were very clear in stating that notices under section 5(1) or 5(1a) are required to be served in the locality and that no such notices were served in the locality. As regards personal service; they limited their claim to the notice under section 5(3) only. 

 26. Besides, both the Courts below have concurrently held that the prayer No. (a) in the instant suit is unnecessary. The appellate Court below held that this prayer is barred by res judicata. In paragraph 3 of the present plaint the plaintiff-opposite parties stated that at the time of requisition or thereafter no notice under section 5(la) and 5(3) was served "either in the locality or on the plaintiffs as required by law for acquisition". The plaintiff- opposite parties never averred that they were entitled to a personal notice under section 5(la). Their prayer No.(a) in the present suit was for a decree declaring that required, legal or valid notices under section 5 (Ia) or 5(3) have not been issued or served in L.A. Case No.63/59-60 in respect of the suit property as rape) visions of law. Surely, this prayer means that no notice under section 5(1a) was served in the manner provided by law itself, i.e. by . causing a public notice to be given at convenient places on or near the requisitioned property stating that the property is proposed to be acquired. 

 28. It has next been contended by the learned Deputy Attorney-General that the plaintiff-opposite parties have not led any evidence in the suit that no public notice was given under section 5(1a) in 1960. P. W. 1, the only witness examined by the plaintiff-opposite parties, has not uttered a word regarding lack of public notice under section 5(1a). The trial Court has taken into account the opinion of the Minister, opinion of the Law Ministry and the note made by the Additional Deputy Commissioner, but these papers were not formally proved by any witness. The makers of these statements were not examined and no one was examined to prove that those were statements made by them. As such, this opinion evidence is absolutely inadmissible and there can be no finding that there was no public notice under section 5(la) in 1960 on the basis of these opinion. Further, the plaintiff-opposite parties could file an application under section 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure for correction of the decree in Title Suit No. 36 of 1968 so as to rectify the decree to the extent that no public notice was given under section 5(1a) and since they failed to do so, they cannot now re-open the matter and they are barred to do so under Order 2, Rule 2(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure. 

 30. Now coming to the concurrent finding by the Courts below that service in 1973 of an alleged copy of an old notice dated 21.6.60 under section 5(1) is no service of notice at all and service of a notice under section 5(3) giving only 7 days’ time to file any objection against acquisition is also no notice under the said Act, we do not find any reason to differ from the concurrent findings of the Court below. The service of the alleged copy of the old notice is no compliance with the provisions of section 5(1a) which is mandatory in nature. Giving 7 days’ notice, when the statute itself provides for 15 days’ notice, is also no notice in terms of the Act itself. Both the notices were issued not defectively or irregularly, but without jurisdiction. A statutory authority required to act by following a set procedure given in the Act itself cannot be said to act with jurisdiction if he deviates therefrom in material particulars. The impugned notices in prayer No.(c) are, therefore, no notices at all in the eye of law, far less notices under Act No. XIII of 1948 and, therefore, we hold that the bar of section 14A has no application in the present case. When a statutory authority acts without jurisdiction or acts in a manner without following a procedure provided in the statute itself, then it is not an act under the statute and the bar of suit does not apply. 

 31. A ground has been taken in the civil provisional application that the validity of acquisition of immovable property under Act No. XIII of 1948 is not dependent upon prior issuance of notice under section 5(la) and 5(3) of the said Act and as such the Court of appeal below committed an error of law in holding that the Gazette Notification dated 25.6.73 was illegal and without jurisdiction. 

 32. We arc of the opinion that it is too late in the day to argue that notices under section 5(1a) and 5(3) of the said Act are not a sine qua non for the validity of the acquisition proceedings under section 5 (7). The Government docs not take a decision to acquire a requisitioned property unless it receives a report from the Deputy Commissioner containing his recommendations on the objections received. The Deputy Commissioner in his turn receives objection from the owners after service of notice in the manner provided under section 5(1 a) and 5(3). He has to hear the objections and has to make further enquiry if any. If notices under section 5(la) and 5(3) are not mandatorily required to be served before the Deputy Commissioner submits his report and the Government takes a decision to acquire the requisitioned properties, then the whole game of compulsory acquisition of private land will be left to the ipse dixit of the executive. A notice under section 5(1a) and 5 (3) is mandatory before the Government can at all decide to acquire any requisitioned property, far less publish a notification to that effect. If no such notices were received or if notices were invalid or illegal then the subsequent acquisition under section 5(7) is also illegal. We concur with the Courts below that the Gazette Notification dated 25.6.73 has no legal basis or validity or binding force and that it is illegal and void. The bar of section 14A is also not applicable to this Gazette Notification 

 33. It has been finally argued by the learned Deputy Attorney-General that the prayer No. (d) in so far as it seeks a mandatory injunction requiring the defendant-petitioners to start a valid acquisition proceeding afresh under Part-Il of section 3 of the Requisition and Acquisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982 and other provisions of law in force for acquisition within three months failing which the possession of the suit land be restored to the plaintiffs, is not maintainable and, therefore, the Court of appeal below committed an illegality in granting the plaintiff-opposite parties the said prayer. 

 34. We find that the defendant-petitioners stated in paragraph 11 of their written statement in the present suit that the plaintiff-opposite parties land measuring an area of 6.4650 acres along with other lands was requisitioned 'on 21.6.60 "with a view to permanent acquisition for Railway Staff Quarter under L.A. Case No. 63/59-60". It has also been stated that the "vacant possession of the land in question was handed over to the Railway Board on 2.7.60 and since then the requiring body is possessing the land after constructing their buildings." 

 35. When it is the defendant-petitioners' own case that the suit land was requisitioned with a view to permanent acquisition for Railway Staff Quarter and when it is their own case that the requiring body is possessing the suit land after constructing their buildings thereon, then they have no right to possess the property as a mere requisitioned property for an indefinite period. They have either to de-requisition the property, dismantle the buildings constructed thereon and hand over the vacant possession thereof to the owners in the same condition in which they came into possession thereof, giving a goodbye to their desire for acquisition, or they have to complete the acquisition proceedings in accordance with the 'law of acquisition as it stands in present, not in accordance with the law as it stood in 1960. The mandatory injunction thus given under the circumstances is the most appropriate and correct decree. The defendant-petitioners cannot Just sit over the property and continue to deny the plaintiff-opposite parties their rightful claim of a proper notice of acquisition of the suit property followed by necessary consequences thereof.
